title: Offshore wind is still on track to triple globally by 2030, despite US uncertainty | Global Offshore Wind Alliance (GOWA)
text:
Offshore wind is still on track to triple globally by 2030, despite US uncertainty | Global Offshore Wind Alliance (GOWA)

 29 October 2025 

# Offshore wind is still on track to triple globally by 2030, despite US uncertainty 

 Global offshore wind targets remain strong enough to support tripling of capacity by 2030, despite the recent slowdowns in the United States. A new analysis by Ember and Global Offshore Wind Alliance (GOWA) shows that the rest of the world is pressing ahead, signaling confidence in offshore wind as a cornerstone of future energy systems. 

Analysis of national, subnational and regional commitments shows that 27 countries, 27 subnational governments and 3 regions have offshore wind targets in place. This global momentum underscores how clear and credible government targets can unlock investment, create market certainty and accelerate the build-out of offshore wind at scale. 

Report: Global offshore wind targets.

The combined 2030 national targets add up to 263 GW, excluding the People's Republic of China, which does not yet have a national target. Europe remains a front runner, with 15 countries targeting 99 GW by 2030. In Asia, countries are rapidly building their pipeline, with India targeting 30-37 GW, Japan aiming for 41 GW in total including 15 GW of floating offshore wind by 2040, while South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam contribute to a combined regional ambition of 41 GW. 

China laid out an ambitious new target this month. On 20 October, the Beijing Declaration 2.0 was signed, which stated annual installed offshore wind power capacity shall be no less than 15 GW offshore wind capacity, during the “15th Five-Year Plan” period (2026-2030). That is almost double the 8 GW average achieved during 2021-2025. In China, 11 coastal provinces have already set 2025 targets totaling 64 GW. 

While 2030 remains an important milestone, governments are looking beyond short-term targets. 18 countries have announced post-2030 goals, reflecting a commitment to long-term integration of offshore wind into their energy systems. In addition, 7 countries have targets for floating offshore wind, which at an earlier pre-commercial stage compared to fixed-bottom, yet holds significant potential. 

The US slowdown stands in contrast to this global trend. While the country has maintained its 30 GW national target for 2030, recent policy reversal and market headwinds have cast doubt on its delivery. At the same time, 11 states have targets of a combined 84 GW of offshore wind, showing that momentum continues at the sub-national level. Around 5.8 GW of offshore wind is still expected to be built in the US between 2025 to 2029, based on the five projects currently under construction. 

Government leadership globally has been fundamental to the scale up of offshore wind so far. But to sustain and expand this growth, more countries with offshore wind potential need to set targets — and those with existing targets must raise their ambition. 

Dave Jones, Chief Analyst at Ember said, “Offshore wind already delivers 83 GW of energy capacity across the world, enough to power 73 million homes. To countries thinking about agreeing new targets or extending existing targets, the message is clear: now is the time to act, to help spur the next wave of growth.” 

Amisha Patel, Head of Secretariat at GOWA added, “Despite recent challenges, the fundamentals of offshore wind energy remain strong. Momentum continues to build as nations advance this proven technology, which is essential to the clean energy transition. Achieving the Paris Agreement goals depends on large-scale offshore wind deployment, as well as providing reassurance to investors and industry. With Brazil joining GOWA at COP28 and assuming the COP30 Presidency, we urge the Presidency to turn ambition into implementation and to recognise offshore wind as a cornerstone of global climate action. 

Aligning targets with timely policy reform and collective action across government and industry will be critical to translating ambition into delivery and ensuring offshore wind fulfills its promise as a pillar of energy security, industrial growth and resilience.
